explanation: The thumbs-up is understood across the UK as a casual, positive signal of approval, agreement, or encouragement, used in everyday conversation and most professional contexts without causing offense. Its positive use in English-speaking countries is long-established, dating at least to the First World War.
local_tip: Use the thumbs-up freely in casual and most professional settings in the UK; it is almost never read as rude.

also_check.note: Historically read by some older Greeks as a vulgar gesture rather than approval, though the positive Western meaning is now widely understood, especially among younger people.
Often used to mean the number 'one' when counting on fingers, which can cause brief confusion rather than offense.
Can be seen as impolite by some in more conservative or older circles, though it is now widely understood and used positively, especially among younger people.
